The question I get most right now is "what should I turn into an AI agent?"

Here is the 5 part test I use (works for Cl
items.content:
The question I get most right now is "what should I turn into an AI agent?"

Here is the 5 part test I use (works for Claude/Codex/Grokbot etc):

1. It has a repeated trigger, so the same kind of task keeps happening over and over.
2. The inputs are stable, so the information comes in a predictable shape every time.
3. The tools are clear, so there is a defined set of things it can actually go do.
4. There is a measurable finish line, so you can tell when it is done and whether it worked.
5. There is judgment in the middle, so each run is a little different and needs a real decision made in the moment.

The first 4 are really just asking "can this be automated at all?" The 5th is the one that matters, because judgment in the middle is what makes it an agent instead of a simple automation.

Once you see it this way, you start spotting agent work pretty much everywhere.

One of the biggest consumer AI opportunities is helping people close the tiny loops they keep avoiding.

Think about the
items.content:
One of the biggest consumer AI opportunities is helping people close the tiny loops they keep avoiding.

Think about the 47 little things sitting on your list that you keep not doing. 

Emailing back the person you owe a reply, disputing the wrong charge, rescheduling the appointment, things like that.

Each one is small, but each one requires digging up context, making a decision, and sending a slightly uncomfortable message. So they just kinda sit there lol.

The opportunity is an agent that does the hard 90% of each loop, finds the context, makes the call, drafts the message, so all you do is hit send.

The wedge is going after one loop first and nailing it.

Examples:

1. Warranty and rebate claims. People throw away hundreds because filing feels like homework. The agent watches your purchases, knows what's claimable, fills the forms, and hands you the check.

2. The "I should switch" loops. You're overpaying for insurance, your phone plan, your electricity, and you know it, but comparing is a slog. The agent monitors and drafts the switch when it's clearly worth it.

3. The kid-logistics loop. The permission slip, the form the school needs signed, the birthday party you never RSVP'd to, the summer camp that's about to fill up. For any parent, it's a hundred tiny deadlines a month, and the agent catches each one and drafts the response.

Things like that. Just giving some ideas to get the creative juices flowing. 

Tons of apps like this will be created over the next 12 months.

It just makes sense.

LLMs are not a path to human-level intelligence.
But they are very useful. 

Generative architectures that produce discr
items.content:
LLMs are not a path to human-level intelligence.
But they are very useful. 

Generative architectures that produce discrete tokens auto-regressively totally suck at modeling natural signals (like video or any high-dimension, continuous, noisy signal) and can't understand the real world.
That's why current AI assistant use separately-trained perception encoders (not LLMs). And that's why future AI systems will use non-generative architectures that operate in continuous representation space.

Agentic system cannot be made reliable and controllable without the ability to predict the consequences of their actions. That's why future intelligent systems will need world models with an ability to use these world models to plan.

Understood?

3) Memory

- The first product is already profitable.

You can spin up an AI workforce with one prompt.

Here's why it works: it pulls the context the AI needs to lay the foundation.

Give it:
- your role
- team size

After that, build it out in four steps:

1) Start with 1 agent.
- What does it feel like to work with one?

2) Make that agent proactive.
- Now it's doing things on your behalf before you ask.

3) Expand to 2 agents.
- One directs the other, or routes to it.
- This is where you learn how context gets passed.

4) Scale the workforce.
- A mission control where you watch it all move around.
- Now you see what has to run in parallel, which agent never needed that tool, which one runs fine on a smaller model.
- Not everything needs Opus. Sub-agents are haiku and sonnet.

The catch: the prompt gets you agents with markdown files doing some stuff. 

Getting to the 90% plus level is iteration, and that part is specific to each person. 

Nobody can hand it to you.

Start with one agent. 

Spin up one agent this week. The rest is discovery.

Stop over organizing Claude. It slows you down.

Here are 20 things to delete (& the 6 to keep):

Delete these today:

1. Your prompt library. You never open it.
2. The 40 skills you used once.
3. Every connector you added "just in case."
4. The 31-page prompting guide (I deleted mine).
5. The hacks you screenshot and never run.
6. Screenshots you collect instead of using Claude.
7. The 2nd subscription you forgot you're paying for.
8. The folders inside folders inside folders.
9. The "perfect setup" you still haven't started.
10. The chat history you'll "go back to read."
11. The YouTube tutorial saved at 3% watched.
12. The custom style you built & never switched on.
13. The project you created, used once, abandoned.
14. Global instructions so long Claude ignores half.
15. Thinking on "high" to ask about the weather.
16. The 6 connectors when you only use Gmail.
17. Skills that overlap with skills.
18. The organized Cowork folder & never opened.
19. Screenshots of other people's prompts.
20. The plugin pack you installed for one task.

Now the only 6 things to keep:

1. One "about-me" file.

One .md file: your role, tone, non-negotiables.
Claude reads it once & stops sounding like Claude. 
This single file beats every saved prompt template.

2. Give Claude the goal, not the steps.

"Write the email in 4 short paragraphs, friendly, no bullet points" = you doing its job. 
Say "reply to this so they say yes" and let it think. 
The more you micromanage, the dumber the output

3. Make it ask YOU questions first.

Add 1 line: "Before you answer, AskUserQuestion." 
Now it interviews you instead of guessing. 
You don't know how to prompt. It does. 
Let it pull the context out of you.

4. Never trust the first answer.

Reply with: "What's wrong with this? Now fix it." 
Claude critiquing Claude beats Claude on the first try. The first draft is a draft, not the answer.

5. Start a fresh chat every time.

A 40-message chat is dragging 39 old messages into every reply - that's why it gets slow, forgetful, & generic. New task = new chat. It's much faster.

6. Hand it the hardest task you have.

Most people give Claude the easy 5-min jobs & do the hard work themselves. Backwards. 
Give it the messy spreadsheet, the dense report, the thing you've been avoiding. That's where it saves you an afternoon, not 30 seconds.

items.content:
The SaaSpocalypse is still at least a few years away 

Here's why the timeline is longer than people predict:

1) Time.
- A CRM rebuild takes about 100 hours today.
- It must fall below 3 hours, in a fun click and drag interface.
-  Replit and Lovable are not at that level yet for that complexity.

2) Bandwidth.
- Ask the most AI-first bank if they rebuilt DocuSign, or parts of Salesforce.
- They can. They did not.
- The answer is that they are already bandwidth constrained.

3) Maintenance.
- I built an app a year and a half ago that only lives on my desktop.
- Someone brought it up on a call yesterday. I opened it. It had errored out.
- I did not want to deal with it.

4) Liability.
- When it breaks, an enterprise wants a person to call and an office to walk into.
- Someone to unblock it. Someone to secure it. Someone to blame.
- I work with Fortune 500 CEOs every single day. No way.

5) Lag.
- Salesforce has relationships with all the AI labs and gets into early testing.
- A new model ships and they have at least a 30 day headstart

The catch: the ease of making, customizing, maintaining and securing must reach 95%+

Until then, companies will keep paying someone else to hold the risk. 

So before you rebuild anything, ask yourself is it worth it?

items.content:
The part of an AI workforce nobody rethinks is the org chart.

Here's why it matters: if you name your agents CMO, chief product officer, front-end engineer, you just rebuilt a 2015 company with 2026 tools. Mine is one AI chief of staff with six directors. 

Build it in 5 parts:

1) Roles.
- Name them for the work, not for the titles that existed in 2015.
- Six directors: education, client work, operations, marketing, product. The sixth isn't a function.

2) The hire you'd never make.
- All of these employees "basically cost zero dollars."
- So at the margin, hire the weirdo.
- Phoebe is the "chief dreaming officer." She sits in the corner and asks how to 10x whatever the other five produce.

3) A watcher.
- Toby's only job is watching the AI workforce work and taking notes on what still has friction and who needs access to what.
- "Every single time you keep correcting this one agent's output, have you thought about giving your agent access to this?"

4) Context.
- Anything not in a meeting, an email, or Slack is invisible to them.
- So AI prompts me daily to dictate the rest — four times faster than writing. Five minutes some days, 40 on others.
- 86 entries in, that's a personal wiki every agent can read.

5) Correction.
- An agent told me Greg confirmed the interview. Greg confirmed, but we were still moving dates over text, and the iMessage MCP was broken.
- It can't see what it can't see, and it will never tell you that.

The catch: this takes months, not days. 

Most of that time isn't building. It's taking stock of assumptions about your own work, the thing you've done for almost 40 years, and being willing to change it. 

So start with the one agent whose output you keep correcting, and go find out what it can't see.

The whole point is to stop being the limiting factor between idea and implementation

items.content:
One of the best jobs you can give an AI right now is to be a watchdog.

Here is why it works: a watchdog reads what is already happening within your org, and finds redundancies, inefficiencies, and synergies.

Start in these 4 places:

1) Slack.
- It reads the channels and finds duplicative work.
- Two people are building the same thing. Now you know on day one.

2) Your calendar.
- It finds the conflicts before you do.

3) Your meetings.
- It listens for disagreements and opportunities that you would have missed

4) Your documents.
- Before the edit, after the edit. Compare and contrast.
- We did this on contracts at a large enterprise 10 years ago, and we called it the greatest use case ever.

Then let your team talk to it.

I have a Slack channel called Loop Alley. A teammate writes in about a large financial services client — "did they respond to Ali's email?" — and my AI workforce answers that person. Nobody waits 5 hours for me.

The catch: it is a mess to set up in this exact moment.

The best practices do not exist yet.

But to get a baseline,  you can ask Claude to interview you, and tell it you want a workforce

The scale
This isn't a small side project - it's a huge, fast-moving repo: 6,810 commits in about 4 months (mid-April 2026 → now), averaging roughly 50+ commits a day. That kind of pace usually means heavy AI-assisted development (the repo even has .claude, .claude-plugin, and .agents folders baked in).

What kind of work it is
Looking at the changelog tags across the whole history:
-> 970 features – new stuff being built
-> 911 fixes – bugs getting squashed
->908 improvements – polish/refinement
->302 infra – backend/deployment work
->194 security – hardening, exploit fixes
->173 docs, 149 sdk – documentation and developer tooling

So it's a healthy mix: not just "adding features," but a lot of active bug-fixing and security tightening too - a sign of a real production system under load, not just a demo.

The story arc (in simple terms)
1. April 2026 – Foundation: Basic pages (sign-in, features, create), wallet login, 3D avatar validation tools, widget system.

The big picture

The project is essentially building a pipeline of: photo/prompt → 3D avatar → AI agent with memory/emotions → on-chain identity → autonomous crypto payments/trading, and it's iterating on all of that live, in public, with a very transparent changelog (they literally publish trading losses/wins and postmortems).

items.content:
the verifier is what separates a loop from an expensive illusion and most loops are missing it

most people build the loop and skip the verifier. they get an agent that runs, produces confident output, and never tells them when it is wrong. that is not a loop. that is an expensive script.

five components run every real loop.

automation makes the loop run. skill gives it project memory. sub-agents give it an independent judge, the maker and checker are never the same agent. connectors let the loop act, not just suggest. verifier is the gate. tests, builds, linters. pass or fail. no opinions.

without automation, nothing starts. without memory, every run starts from zero. without an independent checker, the system grades its own homework. without connectors, it can only tell you what to do. without a verifier, nothing knows whether the work actually survived.

before you build one, all four conditions must be true.

the work recurs at least weekly. something can automatically reject bad output. your token budget can absorb the overhead. the agent has access to its real working environment.

the diagram names where loops fail and most people never read this part.

ralph wiggum loop exits early on incomplete work that looks done. goal drift loses constraints as context gets summarized. agentic laziness settles for good enough and stops pushing. comprehension debt turns unreviewed code today into confusion tomorrow.

the difference is simple. an agent produces. a loop produces, checks, decides, and runs again.

but the interesting part starts when the loop stops improving the output and starts improving itself.

a loop around a loop. the outer loop changes how the inner loop searches. same model at both levels. result: 5x better than a single loop.

the metric that matters is not tasks completed or tokens spent.

cost per accepted change. if you accept less than 50 percent of what the loop produces, the loop is losing.

the question is no longer how good your agent is. it is how well the system around it can keep going.

the loop takes the mechanical work. it does not take the judgment. 95 percent boring and repetitive runs on its own. 5 percent judgment, risk, real decisions. needs you.

you are already paying for a fleet. you are using one chat window.

the leverage shifted. the job shifted.

# Codebase Atlas

Produce a single self-contained HTML page (no external deps, CSP-safe) that maps a repository as
an isometric city: blocks sized by real line counts, edges carrying animated data dots, a left
structure rail, and a right WHAT IT DOES / HOW IT'S BUILT panel. Publish it as an artifact.

## Step 1: Inventory the repo (facts, not guesses)

Spawn an Explore agent (very thorough) asking for a structured inventory:

- 15-35 major subsystems, each with: short name, directory/key files, 1-2 plain-English sentences
for a non-expert, rough size (files or LOC), and what it talks to (directed edges with what flows).
- Overall request flow, databases/storage, headline stats (total LOC, routers/routes, feature
counts, test files, deployed services).
- Ask it to correct your assumed subsystem list, and to distinguish deployed **services** from
code-level **roles** 

Every number shown in the atlas must come from this scan. Never invent counts.

## Step 2: Build from the template engine

Copy `references/atlas-template.html` (the finished CordComputer atlas) into the session scratchpad
and keep the engine; replace only the DATA section near the top of the script:

- `STRUCTURES`: id, 2-char code, name, group, loc label, grid pos `gx,gy`, footprint `w,d`,
height `h` (scale by LOC), `what`, `how`, `talks[]`, optional `children[]` (code, name, h, what)
for go-inside views, optional `slab:true` for flat storage blocks.
- `EDGES`: `{f, t, flow:1}` for animated main-path edges, `dashed:1` for advisory/CI edges,
`pay` names what travels (shown when hovering a dot), optional `via:[[gx,gy]...]` waypoints.
- `EXTERNALS`: off-map labels with dashed leaders (LLM providers, SaaS APIs, uploads).
- `TRACE`: 10-14 `[structId, sentence]` steps walking one canonical request end to end.
- Topbar stats, sidebar `GROUPS`, and the two overview essays (`OVERVIEW_WHAT`, `OVERVIEW_HOW`).

Layout rules that make it read well:

- Iso projection is `x=(gx-gy)*26, y=(gx+gy)*14.3 - h*16`. Keep block footprints disjoint;
painter order sorts by `gx+gy` so nothing needs z-hacks.
- Cluster by zone: browser surfaces top, API below them, agent right, ingestion left, core domain
center, compute below it, storage slabs bottom row, CI in a corner.
- Default edge routing is an L-elbow; add `via` waypoints only when a line would cut through an
unrelated cluster. Lines hidden under blocks are acceptable.
- Biggest subsystem = tallest block. Storage = flat slabs. The eye should find the core domain
in the middle.

## Step 3: Verify headlessly before publishing

The template has a URL-hash debug hook. Screenshot at 1800x1000 with
`npx --yes playwright screenshot` against `file://...` for at least: the default view, one
`#inside=<id>` view, and `#trace=7`. Look for label collisions, external labels clipping,
orphaned blocks, and edges slicing through clusters. Fix, reshoot, then publish the artifact
(favicon 🗺️, keep it stable across republish).

## Step 4: Share-safety pass (always, before the user posts it)

The atlas may leave the company. Keep code structure (module names, LOC, stack); scrub anything
that describes live infrastructure: concrete cloud service/queue names, public endpoint paths,
API-key prefixes or formats, where credentials are stored, project IDs, resource shapes. Grep the
final file for the company's cloud naming prefix, `@`, `secret`, key prefixes, and mount paths.
Remind the user the artifact stays private until they share it from the page menu.
